title: China Adds AI, Solar and Biotech to Export-Control List as EU Weighs a Trade 'Kill Switch'
subhead: Beijing proposed restricting outbound exports of AI, biopharmaceutical and photovoltaic technology on Friday, hours after EU leaders backed developing a tool that could rapidly eject Chinese firms from the single market — a simultaneous tightening from both directions.

sections.heading: Beijing Moves to Put AI, Solar and Biotech on the Export-Control List
sections.body:
Chinese authorities on Friday proposed adding artificial intelligence, biopharmaceuticals and photovoltaic (solar) technologies to the country's export-control list, according to Nikkei Asia. The stated aim is to stop certain capabilities from 'proliferating inappropriately.'

The proposal is notable for what it targets: not raw materials or finished hardware but process and know-how in three sectors where China has built genuine industrial strength — solar manufacturing, biotech, and increasingly frontier AI. It follows years of US-led restrictions on advanced chips and chipmaking tools reaching China, and signals Beijing is willing to use its own technological leverage in the same way.

Because this is a proposal rather than a finalized list, the specific controlled items and timelines are not yet public. What is clear is the direction: export controls are becoming a two-way instrument, with both Washington and Beijing now restricting the outward flow of technology as well as the inward flow of hardware.
sections.whyItMatters: If finalized, this gives China a formal lever over AI/solar/biotech exports — the mirror image of US chip controls. It hardens the split between two technology ecosystems and puts multinationals doing joint R&D in China on notice.

sections.heading: EU Leaders Back a Trade 'Kill Switch' Aimed at Chinese Firms
sections.body:
EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday voiced broad support for developing a powerful new trade instrument that could include a 'kill switch' — a mechanism to quickly eject Chinese companies from the EU single market, the South China Morning Post reported, citing people briefed on the talks. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen signalled her trade team could begin work on it, and leaders requested a proposal by year-end, per Bloomberg.

The tool builds on a French-German joint paper from the previous week and follows record EU-China trade deficits driven by a surge of low-cost Chinese imports. Beijing responded sharply, warning Brussels not to 'fantasise' that a hard line would force concessions — exactly a week after the two sides struck a surprise deal to limit Chinese hybrid-car shipments to Europe.

Chinese officials also framed the measure as partly aimed at telecoms suppliers, pointing to protectionist motives rather than pure trade-balance concerns.
sections.whyItMatters: A formal EU exclusion mechanism would be the bloc's most aggressive trade weapon yet, and its first designed explicitly around tech and industrial overcapacity. Combined with Beijing's own export-control push, it marks a shift from tariff skirmishes to institutional tools that can remove firms from whole markets.

sections.heading: Intel CEO Says Washington Won't Meddle as US, Nvidia, SoftBank Hold Stakes
sections.body:
In an exclusive interview with Nikkei Asia, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the Trump administration has 'any policy' to use its minority stake in Intel to interfere in the company's business strategy — defending a structure in which the US government, SoftBank Group and Nvidia have all taken equity positions in the chipmaker to support its recovery.

Tan also assessed that chips made in China are 'not far behind' US technology, a candid public acknowledgment that the gap in some segments is narrowing despite years of export controls.

The arrangement is unusual: Nvidia — a competitor — holding equity in Intel, with the state as a co-investor, raises questions about coordination, competitive neutrality and whether strategic direction is being set by the market or by policy. Tan's insistence that there is no interference is precisely the reassurance the market wants, but the underlying question of state influence over a private chipmaker remains open.
sections.whyItMatters: A US government equity stake in a flagship chipmaker, alongside a rival's investment, is new territory for semiconductor industrial policy. Tan's 'not far behind' remark also undercuts the assumption that controls alone have frozen China's chip progress.

sections.heading: Japan's Grid Exposed Through 100 Million Home Devices
sections.body:
Nikkei Asia reports that cyberactors seeking to disrupt Japan's electricity supply face tens of millions of potential entry points through the growing network of residential devices connected to the grid — specifically smart meters and home battery/storage systems. Researchers warn that attackers could attempt to simultaneously disable grid-connected home batteries, potentially triggering an extensive blackout.

The vulnerability is a structural feature of grid modernization: as distributed energy resources are networked for efficiency and demand management, they become a distributed attack surface. Japan's push to add residential storage and smart-metering at scale is precisely what widens the exposure.
sections.whyItMatters: Grid-edge devices are becoming a critical-infrastructure attack vector, not a side issue. Defending the grid increasingly means securing millions of consumer devices, not just utility control rooms.

sections.heading: Ukrainian Drones Hit Russian Data Centres, Disrupting Digital Services
sections.body:
Long-range Ukrainian strike drones targeted Russian data centres, causing various Russian digital services and apps to go down or face severe disruption, according to Tom's Hardware. The report notes some indication that online bot activity may have fallen, though by less than initial accounts claimed.

Data centres have become a physical, not just logical, target in the war — a shift that matters well beyond this conflict. A concentrated facility that hosts a country's apps and services is simultaneously an economic asset and a single point of failure. The attacks highlight how physical fragility of digital infrastructure can translate directly into service outages.
sections.whyItMatters: Nation-state and military targeting of commercial data centres sets a precedent: cloud and data-centre operators are now de facto infrastructure under threat, with implications for redundancy, siting and insurance well outside Russia.

sections.heading: Taiwan Builds a $4bn Industrial Park in Texas, and a Chip Supply-Chain Attack on US Courts
sections.body:
Taiwan is raising US$4 billion to build an industrial park in Texas intended to help smaller Taiwanese manufacturers follow TSMC and Foxconn into the US, per Tom's Hardware. Many of these suppliers cannot afford standalone US sites, so the park is designed to lower the barrier to relocating a slice of Taiwan's dense supply chain alongside advanced fabs — a concrete step in building a US-side ecosystem rather than just fab capacity.

Separately, The Register reports that an attack on a BAE-managed system disrupted US bankruptcy courts, a reminder that third-party-managed public-sector IT remains a soft target. The two stories sit at opposite ends of the same theme: states and firms are physically and digitally re-siting and defending the infrastructure that underpins technology supply chains.
sections.whyItMatters: Moving suppliers — not just fabs — is what makes onshoring real. Meanwhile, the courts attack shows the same supply chain's managed-service layer is a live vulnerability.

bottomLine: Friday's defining development was symmetrical: Beijing proposed adding AI, solar and biotech to its export-control list, while EU leaders backed a tool that could eject Chinese firms from the single market — both sides moving from tariffs and hardware bans toward institutional mechanisms that restrict technology flows and market access directly. Alongside this, Intel's CEO defended an unprecedented state-and-rival equity structure while conceding Chinese chips are 'not far behind,' Taiwan put US$4bn toward moving its supplier base to Texas, and attacks on Russian data centres and a BAE-managed system showed that digital infrastructure is now treated as a physical target. Watch for the EU proposal by year-end and the final contents of China's control list — those two documents will define the next phase of tech decoupling.
sources: Nikkei Asia, South China Morning Post, Tom's Hardware, The Register, Reuters, Bloomberg (via SCMP)
